content: Leaders in clinical settings may choose to provide feedback to clinicians regarding the percentage of acute bronchitis visits during which antibiotics were prescribed. This feedback can include comparisons with the prescribing percentages of their peers. Such an approach, which involves tracking and reporting data for high-priority conditions, has been shown to reduce inappropriate antibiotic prescribing and improve the selection of antibiotics. One method of measurement involves calculating the number of antibiotics prescribed by a clinician for all diagnoses, divided by the total number of visits for all diagnoses by that clinician. Providing clinicians with individualized prescribing percentages, compared to their peers, has been effective in reducing antibiotic prescribing. This strategy can also help mitigate the impact of variations in diagnostic coding practices among clinicians. A phenomenon known as diagnosis shifting occurs when a clinician alters a diagnostic code to justify prescribing an antibiotic. For instance, a clinician might record a diagnosis of pneumonia (which requires antibiotics) when the patient actually has acute bronchitis (which does not require antibiotics). Tracking the percentage of all visits that result in antibiotic prescriptions is less susceptible to manipulation through diagnosis shifting compared to tracking specific conditions like acute bronchitis. Clinicians who care for a higher proportion of immunosuppressed patients may have different prescribing patterns compared to their peers. Additionally, adverse outcomes such as Clostridioides difficile infections, drug interactions, and other adverse drug events, as well as trends in antibiotic resistance among common outpatient bacterial pathogens, should be monitored. However, at the individual or clinic level, smaller sample sizes may reduce the reliability or utility of these measures. In such cases, investigating C. difficile infections to assess potential links to prior outpatient visits and antibiotic prescriptions can serve as a marker for adverse drug events. Both clinicians and clinic leaders play a role in antibiotic stewardship. Clinicians can track and report their own antibiotic prescribing practices by engaging in activities such as self-evaluation of their prescribing habits. This self-assessment allows clinicians to align their practices with updated evidence-based recommendations and clinical guidelines. Additionally, participation in continuing medical education and quality improvement activities can help clinicians monitor and improve their antibiotic prescribing. These activities can be tailored to specific clinical specialties and may also fulfill licensure and other professional requirements. Outpatient clinic or healthcare system leaders can implement antibiotic prescribing tracking and reporting systems. These systems can focus on high-priority conditions identified as areas for improvement, the percentage of all visits leading to antibiotic prescriptions, and, for health systems, complications of antibiotic use and trends in antibiotic resistance. If antibiotic prescribing outcomes are already being tracked, these data can be used to further refine stewardship efforts. Education on appropriate antibiotic use is essential and can target both patients and clinicians. Educating patients and their families can enhance health literacy and support efforts to improve antibiotic use. For clinicians and clinic staff, education can reinforce appropriate prescribing practices and improve the overall quality of care. However, deficits in clinician knowledge are rarely the sole barrier to appropriate antibiotic prescribing in outpatient settings.
